title: Two Cards as One
description: The double lift: show one card, deal another, and make a card change
tryIt: Practise the double lift ten times with a known pair on top (the face you show must always be the second card), then perform The Changing Card for one person.

concepts.title: How it works: show one, deal another
concepts.contentHtml:
A double lift turns two cards over as though they were one. You square the top two cards of the deck so neatly that they pass for a single card, turn them face up together, and show the face of the lower one while the top card hides behind it. Turn them face down again and the card that is really on top is still the card you started with. You showed one card and dealt another. Show one, mean another: that is the whole idea, and everything in this skill grows from it.

The idea is old. In 1584 Reginald Scot taught a trick that turns four aces into four knaves. In Scot's words the performer is "shewing to the standers by the nether card (which is the ace or kept card) covering also the head or peece of the knave (which is the next card) with your foure fingers, draw out the same knave,1 laieng it downe on the table." The audience sees an ace; the card on the table is the knave beside it. The hands are quite different from a double lift, but the bargain is the same: one card on show, another in play.

Erdnase's 1902 manual gives the family a name. His chapter on changes promises "several of the best methods known for secretly exchanging one or several cards separated from the pack, for others in the pack or held in the other hand". A double lift is the gentlest member of that family, because nothing leaves the deck and nothing is hidden in your hand: two cards simply pass for one. The only skill is making the squared pair look like what the audience expects to see, a single card.

concepts.title: The method: The Changing Card
concepts.contentHtml:
A card is shown, dealt face down, and changes into a different card at a snap of the fingers. Before you start, put the 7♦ on top of the deck with the K♠ directly beneath it. Nothing else is needed.

  1. Break. Hold the deck face down in your left hand. As your right hand squares the ends, press the tip of your left little finger into the gap at the inner right corner, under the top two cards, so a tiny gap stays there. Practise with two known cards on top until the break always sits under exactly two.
  2. Lift. Take the two cards above the break between your right thumb and fingers, squeezed as one, and turn them face up like the page of a book. Lay them squared on the deck. Everyone sees the K♠.
  3. Show. Say "the king of spades" and leave it there for a breath. A rush draws the eye.
  4. Return. Turn the pair face down the same way and square them on the deck. The 7♦ is on top again.
  5. Deal. Take the top card, the 7♦, and lay it face down on the table. Ask someone to rest a hand on it: "the king of spades".
  6. Change. Snap your fingers, ask them to turn it over: it is the 7♦. As a bonus, turn over the top card of the deck: the K♠ has swapped places with it.

What they see is one king shown and one card dealt. What you do is show the second card and deal the first. Common mistakes are a break so wide that it flashes at the side, looking at your hands as you lift, turning the pair faster than you would turn a single card, and a break under one card or three instead of two. Handle the pair exactly as you would handle one card and it will pass for one.

concepts.title: Myth check: it has to be fast
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A double lift only works if your hands are very fast.
Reality It works when you handle two cards exactly as you would handle one: slowly, openly and without looking at them.

Scot's 1584 trick shows why speed is not the point. When the performer is done, he says, "The beholders all this while thinking that there lie foure aces on the table, are greatlie abused, and will marvell at the transformation.1" Nobody was fooled by a blur. They were fooled by what they assumed: they saw an ace and took it for the only card in play.

Wait, really? A double lift does the same, and a hurried one defeats it. A person who has no reason to doubt a card never counts it, but a hand that hesitates, a pair held with too much care, or a sudden snatch gives them a reason. So the practice goal is dull on purpose: turn two cards as casually as you would turn one, until the move is boring even to you.

title: The Rising Card
description: A routine built on the double lift: their card is lost in the middle and rises to the top
tryIt: Practise the Rising Card on your own until the cut-at-the-crimp, the break and the lift flow without a pause, then perform it for one person.

concepts.title: How it works: lost in the middle, back on top
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the best-loved effects in card magic is the ambitious card: a card is pushed into the middle of the deck and, however deep you bury it, it jumps back to the top. The version you can do now joins the key card from the first skill to the double lift. The spectator picks a card and you lose it with the same cuts as in Feel the Key: the crimped key card lies directly on the chosen card, and any number of cuts leaves them neighbours.

The new step is to cut the deck at the crimp instead of dealing through it. A cut only turns the ring of cards, so the crimped key card becomes the top card and the chosen card is second from top. Now a double lift shows the second card, which is the spectator's own card, face up, with the key card hidden behind it. Turn the pair face down and push the top card into the middle. It is the key card, not their card, so their card is now the real top card.

Notice how honest the first half is: they see their real card. The trick lives in the second half, where what they think they buried is not what they showed. Pailhès and Kuhn, psychologists at Goldsmiths, University of London, say why this feels like magic: the audience experiences wonder because they erroneously attribute a magical cause, rather than the true cause (the secret method), to what they have just seen.1 Your job is to supply an attractive wrong cause, such as a card that is simply very ambitious.

concepts.title: The method: The Rising Card
concepts.contentHtml:
You need the crimp from Feel the Key and two skills from this lesson: cutting at a key, and the double lift. In the example the crimped key is the 7♣ and the spectator chooses the Q♥. You never need to know the Q♥ beforehand.

  1. Set up. Crimp a corner of the bottom card (the 7♣). Have a card chosen, lose it with the cut-and-cover of Feel the Key and let them cut as often as they like. The Q♥ lies directly under the 7♣.
  2. Find the crimp. Spread the deck face down between your hands, eyes on the spectator, until you see the curled corner. Cut so the crimped card becomes the top card and press the curl flat as you square up. The deck now runs 7♣, Q♥, and then the rest.
  3. Break. Take a little-finger break under the top two cards.
  4. Lift. Turn the pair face up: "Is this your card?" They see the Q♥ and say yes. Show it slowly.
  5. Bury. Turn the pair face down. Take the top card, the 7♣, and push it into the middle of the deck: "Let's lose it right in the middle."
  6. Rise. Ask a question, tap the top of the deck and turn the top card over: the Q♥.

What they see is their card, lost in the middle and found on top. What you do is bury a different card. A common mistake is a crimp that stays visible on the top card as you lift: flatten it. Another is rushing the push-in, which makes it look like a sleight; give it the lazy confidence of a magician who has nothing to hide.

concepts.title: Myth check: misdirection means looking away
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Misdirection means making everyone look away from your hands.
Reality The commonest form is social: you ask a question and hold eye contact, and people simply do not watch.

Pailhès and Kuhn describe it. A common way to divert attention from the deck, they write, is to ask the spectator a question whilst establishing eye contact. They cite earlier work by Kuhn and colleagues (2016) showing that this form of social misdirection prevents people from noticing highly salient changes in their environment,1 such as the back of playing cards changing from blue to red.

Wait, really? A colour changing on an object in front of you, and nobody sees it. That is why the Rising Card asks you to ask your question as the key card is pushed in, not before and not after: the moment of the move is the moment of the question, and your eyes stay on theirs. The technique is gentle, and it works because people expect a conversation and so they spend their attention on it.

title: The Classic Force
description: Offering cards so that the one you want arrives under their finger, and why people feel free
tryIt: Crimp a card, spread the deck and run the Spread Force three times for a friend, with a slip of paper, and count how many times the right card is touched.

concepts.title: How it works: a choice that is not quite a choice
concepts.contentHtml:
A force lets a spectator make a choice that feels free while you already know the answer. The classic force is the oldest: you offer cards, they reach for one, and the card you want arrives under their fingers at the right moment. Reginald Scot taught it in 1584. His performer keeps the card in view and, when the spectator's hand is ready to draw, is told to "put it a little out towards his hand, nimblie turning over the cards, as though you numbred them,1 holding the same more loose and open than the rest, in no wise suffering him to draw anie other."

Erdnase gives a modern recipe in a section called Forcing: fan the deck toward the spectator, and when they show interest in a card, stop the movement, with the located card exposed a trifle more than the others.2 He adds a practical tip: if two or three cards are noted and located together, the force becomes simpler, because you can allow more freedom and still know what was taken.

Psychologists have tested it. Shalom and colleagues, who tested it in 2013, call it the classic force and note that it has been used by stage magicians for centuries. Their question was not whether it works every time, because it does not. It was whether the spectator can tell. A force does not take the choice away; it tilts the table, and the spectator is the last person to notice.

concepts.title: The method: The Spread Force
concepts.contentHtml:
You will need a card you already know, the force card, and a slip of paper. In the example it is the 9♦. This is an effect about a choice that feels free; you are presenting a puzzle and not claiming any powers.

  1. Prepare. Crimp a corner of the 9♦ as in Feel the Key and slip it about a third of the way down the deck. Write "9♦" on a slip, fold it and put it where everyone can see it.
  2. Spread. Hold the deck face down in your left hand and push the cards across with your left thumb in a slow, even ribbon, backs to the spectator and faces to you. You can see the curl, so you know where the 9♦ is.
  3. Invite. "Touch any card you like, and change your mind as often as you wish." Keep the same easy pace.
  4. Steer. As their finger comes down, ease the 9♦ forward a few millimetres so it is exposed a trifle more than its neighbours, and let the spread settle under their touch.
  5. Take. They take the card they touched, look at it and keep it to themselves.
  6. Reveal. Open the slip: 9♦. If the finger heads for another card instead, close the spread, give it a light shuffle and offer it again.

What they see is a spread, a free touch and a card that matches the slip. What you do is hold the pace steady and move the force card where the finger is going. Mistakes: pushing the card out so far that it looks pushed, stopping the spread dead on it, and being wedded to the card: it is much better to close up and try again than to argue with a finger.

concepts.title: Myth check: a force always works
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A force works every time, and a spectator who was forced knows it.
Reality In one controlled test the classic force worked about half the time, and spectators who were forced felt about as free as those who were not.

Shalom and colleagues compared a visual force with the classic force. Their report reads: "Visual and classical psychological forcing was effective respectively for 14 (45%) and 17 (54%) out of 31 participants." So the classic force worked for 17 of the 31 spectators, a little over half, which is why working magicians keep a second plan: close the spread and offer again.

Wait, really? Spectators were asked how free they felt, and those who were forced gave similar ratings to those who were not. The authors sum up: "Our data showed a marked blindness in the introspection of free choice." In other words, you cannot tell from the inside whether your choice was yours.

title: The Cross-Cut Force
description: The Criss-Cross force: a free cut that cannot change the card, and why people believe it
tryIt: Learn the Criss-Cross Force until you can cross the cards and lift without hesitating, then perform it for someone who has never seen it.

concepts.title: How it works: a free cut that changes nothing
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every force steers the choice. An outcome force leaves the choice completely free and makes sure it cannot matter. The best known is the Criss-Cross force, also called the cross-cut force, and it has been studied by Alice Pailhès and Gustav Kuhn at Goldsmiths, University of London. Their description is short: "The spectator is asked to freely cut a deck of cards wherever they want1". The cut is real. It simply has no effect on the card they end up with, which is the top card of the deck from the very start.

You can see why from the piles. The spectator cuts the deck into a top pile, A, and a bottom pile, B. The card you want sits on top of A, and nothing they did could change that, since their cut only decided how many cards were in A. You then lay B across A in a cross. That is the only action that matters. The old top of the deck now lies under B, at the join of the two piles, and the audience, who remember a cut and a cross, assume that the card at the join must be the card they cut to.

The researchers tested it on 60 people in their first experiment and report that participants cannot tell the difference between a forced and a controlled outcome.2 Some were given the card they genuinely cut to, others a card forced by the Criss-Cross, and all rated their sense of control; the two could not be told apart. Like the classic force, it feels free from the inside.

concepts.title: The method: The Criss-Cross Force
concepts.contentHtml:
You need to know the top card of the deck. You can learn it by glimpse: as you square the deck, tilt the top corner up and read it. In the example it is the 5♠. Write "5♠" on a slip and fold it, as in the Spread Force.

  1. Cut. Put the deck on the table. "Cut off a pile anywhere you like and put it to the right." The pile cut off is A, with the 5♠ on top. What remains is B. If they cut nothing, ask again.
  2. Cross. Pick up B and lay it crosswise on A: "to mark where you cut".
  3. Pause. Chat, hold eye contact and ask a question about their cutting habits. Nothing needs to be hidden; the pause only makes the cross feel like old news.
  4. Lift. Lift B away: "so that we can see the card you cut to".
  5. Take. Point at the top card of A, the 5♠, and let them pick it up and look at it, face to them.
  6. Reveal. Open the slip: 5♠.

Work it through with a real order: the deck runs 5♠, 2♦, J♣, 9♥ and so on. If they cut after the fourth card, A is 5♠, 2♦, J♣, 9♥ and B is the rest. B goes across A; lifting B off leaves the 5♠ on top of A. If they cut after one card, A is the 5♠ alone. It works for every cut from 1 to 51 cards. Mistakes: flipping B over as you lift it, glancing at the bottom card of A, or telling them to remember where they cut.

concepts.title: Myth check: it needs a big distraction
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A force like this only works if you distract the spectator at the key moment.
Reality Pailhès and Kuhn tested that belief and found it is false for the Criss-Cross.

Magicians have long taught that the pause between the cross and the lift is a piece of misdirection. In the second experiment, with 90 people, the researchers found that misdirection does not play a role in the success of the force.1 Taking the misdirection away did not weaken the force.

Wait, really? In a third experiment the backs of the cards were numbered, so the spectators had everything they needed to follow what happened to the piles. Even so, only 17% of them realized that their actions had no impact on the outcome.2 The authors suggest an attribute substitution error: a complex and unusual way of cutting the cards is replaced in the spectator's mind by a simpler one, an ordinary cut that the spectator thinks produced the card. So keep your patter: it is good manners, but the force does not depend on it.

title: Pick a Number
description: The 10 to 19 count force, and what research says about choices that feel free
tryIt: Set up the 10 to 19 Count Force with the top card tenth from the top, then ask a friend to think of a number from 10 to 19 and see where their count lands.

concepts.title: How it works: two kinds of free choice
concepts.contentHtml:
Researchers sort forces into two kinds. A choice force covertly influences which card the person picks, like the classic force. An outcome force leaves the choice free and makes it irrelevant, like the Criss-Cross. This lesson adds a force of the second kind, plus a famous test of the first.

In 2015 Jay Olson, Alym Amlani, Amir Raz and Ronald Rensink tested what Pailhès and Kuhn call the Visual Force, a technique that consists of riffling through a deck of cards in front of a spectator1's eyes while asking them to mentally pick one they see. The target card is shown a little longer than the others, which makes it more salient. Olson ran it with 118 people in a street test. McGill University's summary of the results reads: "Some 98% of participants chose the target card; but nine in 10 reported feeling they had a free choice.2"

That is a vivid gap between what happened and what people felt. It gives us a useful vocabulary: a choice can be subjectively free, in that the person feels free, without being objectively free, in that nothing about the card was left to chance. Olson's own summary is plain: "We found that people tend to choose options that are more salient or attention-grabbing, but they don't know why.3" The same habit helps every force in this skill.

concepts.title: The method: The 10 to 19 Count Force
concepts.contentHtml:
This one is nearly self-working. The spectator names a number from 10 to 19, deals that many cards and adds the number's digits; the card they land on is always the card you set up. In the example the top card is the 8♥, which you glimpse as you square the deck.

  1. Set. Glimpse the top card (the 8♥). Then deal ten cards one at a time into a pile on the table, and drop that pile back on top of the deck. Dealing reverses the pile, so the 8♥ is now the tenth card from the top.
  2. Choose. "Think of a number between 10 and 19." Not 20, and not a single digit. Say they choose 13.
  3. Deal. Deal that many cards, 13, face down into a pile on the table. Again the pile reverses.
  4. Add. "Add the two digits of your number together": 1 + 3 = 4.
  5. Count. "Count down that many cards in your pile and take that card." They lift the fourth card down, and look.
  6. Reveal. Show your slip or name the card: 8♥.

Why it works: after dealing n cards the card at depth d from the top of the pile was number n − d + 1 in the deck. For a number from 10 to 19 the digit sum is d = n − 9, so the card is number n − (n − 9) + 1 = 10, which is where you put the force card. Try it with a deck for every number from 10 to 19: it lands on the force card each time. For 20 the digits sum to 2, which lands on the 19th card; for 9 or less it lands on the first. So keep to the range. Mistakes: letting them choose 20, and dealing cards in blocks instead of one at a time.

concepts.title: Myth check: if it felt free, it was free
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth If you felt that you chose freely, then you did.
Reality Feeling free and being free are different things, and the first is a poor guide to the second.

Shalom and colleagues, who tested forcing in live stage magic, define the idea neatly: the word forcing is used in stage magic to describe the act in which a subject reports to have made a free decision among equal possibilities while being manipulated. Olson's 2015 numbers show how wide the gap can be: 98 per cent chose the target, and about nine in ten of them felt free.

Wait, really? Olson's team also used a staged trick to study how it feels to be influenced. In a 2016 study, volunteers were told that a machine could put a number into their mind. As the British Psychological Society's Research Digest put it, "Hidden from the participants was the fact that the experiment was actually conducted in a mock scanner1". The scanner was a prop, and the effect was a trick built into a controlled experiment: the craft of the stage doubles as a research tool.
